title: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Habitual use and disuse of parts produce inherited changes in domestic animals; for example, domestic ducks have lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones relative to the skeleton than wild ducks because they fly less and walk more.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I find in the domestic duck that the bones of the wing weigh less and the bones of the leg more, in proportion to the whole skeleton, than do the same bones in the wild-duck; and I presume that this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more, than its wild parent.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Effects of Habit”. Scope: domesticated animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The inherited acquired-effect mechanism has a clear experimental test, and some relevant data are public. Existing comparative skeleton data alone cannot identify use and disuse as the cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test whether parental use or disuse predicts offspring skeletal traits after controlling offspring activity, genotype and maternal environment, ideally across pedigrees or reciprocal interventions. Inheritance of the acquired shift supports the claim; disappearance under controls refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Few public multigenerational intervention datasets exist.

Domestic-wild differences reflect genetic selection and development.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Museum and scan portals make the duck bone comparison a restricted, partly compilable test, and the same portals thin out quickly for other domestic animals. They do not separate use-inheritance from selection or from rearing conditions, which is the mechanistic content. Discriminating that mechanism would take breeding designs that are not sitting in a public dataset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare wing-bone and leg-bone proportions, scaled to the whole skeleton, between domestic ducks and wild mallards, and extend the same use-matched contrast to other domestic species with known activity differences. A skeletal shift in the predicted direction would support the phenotypic example; inheritance of an acquired effect of use would require offspring of exercised and unexercised parents to differ when the offspring themselves share the same activity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A domestic-wild difference is equally expected under selection on standing variation and under phenotypic plasticity.

A design that isolates inheritance of acquired use from selection is essentially absent from open archives.

Specimen databases record that a skeleton exists more often than they record bone weights.
